# One Workflow, Two Very Different Countries: Mapping Cropland at 30 m on Earth Engine

A recent study mapped cropland in China and Australia at 30 m resolution, using a single workflow on Google Earth Engine. The real story is the method, not the maps. The maps are the output, but the lasting contribution is a process that can be applied, checked and repeated. The claim this piece must earn is that one consistent approach can map cropland accurately in places that have almost nothing in common.

## A deliberately hard pair

China and Australia were chosen because they sit at opposite ends of the farming spectrum. China's cropland is small, fragmented and intensively worked, with plots packed into complicated landscapes. Australia is the opposite extreme. A workflow that succeeds in one of these settings might simply be tuned to it. Succeeding in both is a stronger test. Transferability is the bet: if the same method holds up across such different conditions, it has a good chance of working elsewhere.

## Resolution and time

Resolution matters first. Coarse pixels fail on small fields, blending crops with whatever lies around them and blurring the boundaries that matter most in fragmented landscapes. At 30 m, individual fields can be resolved, which makes a map of small-plot farming realistic.

Time matters just as much. The key idea is that cropland is defined by behavior over a season, not by how a single image looks. Fields are planted, grow, are harvested and may sit bare, and that cycle is what separates them from other land. So the workflow builds seasonal composites and feeds them to the classifier. The classifier sees how the land changes through the growing season, not a single frozen moment, and that is what lets it distinguish cropland from look-alikes.

## Why it scales

The old barrier was practical. Mapping at this resolution over entire countries meant downloading and managing huge volumes of imagery, which put the work out of reach for many teams.

Google Earth Engine changes that. Compute goes to the data rather than the data going to the user, so the heavy lifting happens where the imagery already lives. That makes the workflow portable, since others can run it, and refreshable, since it can be rerun as new imagery arrives.

The classifier is a random forest, chosen for predictability rather than novelty. It is a well-understood method whose behavior is easy to anticipate, and for a workflow meant to travel between countries, that reliability is worth more than something new.

Accuracy claims also need to be honest. The study assessed its maps with independent validation, meaning the results were tested against data not used to build them. That guards against flattering numbers and gives readers a fairer sense of how far the maps can be trusted.

## What a binary map can't tell you

These maps show extent only: land is either cropland or it is not. They say nothing about crop type, irrigation or intensity, all of which matter for many questions. Users should be clear about what a binary map can and cannot support.

The real bottleneck is reference samples. Training and validating a classifier depends on trustworthy examples of what is and isn't cropland, and gathering them is harder than running the code. Cloud gaps add a further limit, since missing observations weaken the seasonal picture the method relies on.

## The payoff: one definition everywhere

The stakes are concrete, and water is a good example. In both countries, decisions about how much water farming uses depend on knowing where the cropland actually is. A single definition of cropland, applied the same way in China and Australia, means the two can finally be compared on equal terms. That consistency enables comparisons that national statistics, each built on its own definitions, cannot offer.

A new study published in Nature Sustainability by the WHEATlab, led by Zhengdong Wang, explores the potential for automatic identification of croplands at 30 m spatial resolution across Australia and China using Earth Engine and global scale composites of satellite data. This paper is not really about the maps that were produced, but about the methodology that was developed. The main claim of this paper is that the developed method is scalable, fast, automated, transferable, robust, and with low error rates. However, the maps that were produced as a result are a direct way to prove this claim.

The maps produced in this study demonstrate the transferability of the method to distinct landscapes across two very different countries, both of which contain highly fragmented cropland patterns. The results also demonstrate the significant reduction in mapping error when using new cloud-based computing solutions that give researchers the ability to allocate computation to the data, rather than the data to the computation. Researchers from the University of Missouri and the University of Arizona are working together to determine how best to utilize the massive amount of data collected by modern satellites in order to achieve the most accurate and consistent global scale maps of cropland possible.

The map products created in this study show that cropland is not a static entity, but rather a dynamic component of the landscape that is constantly changing, and it can be characterized with a high degree of accuracy and computational efficiency using the Earth Engine platform. Researchers are hopeful that these maps will help produce more accurate global scale estimates of crop production and food security, which can then be used to inform policymakers and the general public.

A new study published in Remote Sensing of the Environments explores a novel approach for identifying croplands and other vegetation types across the planet at a resolution of 30 meters using Landsat satellite imagery.

## A deliberately hard pair

The study’s authors, led by Wenhong Ma at the Earth-System Research and the Water and Land Remote Sensing Research group at the Dalian university in China, wanted to test the transferability of their method to countries with very different agricultural practices. As Ma notes, “In terms of land use, China and Australia are the two extremes.” The croplands in Australia are large, mostly contiguous, and managed at relatively low intensity. In China, the croplands are small, fragmented, and intensively managed.

## Resolution and time

The challenge for any algorithm trying to identify croplands is that the distinction between croplands and non-croplands can be subtle. And the lower the resolution of the imagery, the more likely that the line between croplands and non-croplands will fall on the wrong side. Ma writes, “It is difficult to accurately identify the croplands because of the confusion between croplands and grasslands.” This is because “the two are highly mixed and the pixels are very similar in the optical images.” Resolving this challenge is a key reason why the authors choose a 30 m pixel size. Their hypothesis is that the repetitive nature of crop planting and harvesting, combined with the seasonality of the vegetation that distinguishes between croplands and grasslands, will be visible in the satellite imagery. By taking a series of images at different times of year and then assembling the images into seasonal composites, the task of identifying croplands becomes much easier. In a sense, the repetitive and seasonal nature of croplands transform croplands into a behavior, rather than a color.

## Why it scales

The authors’ approach is made possible by Google Earth Engine, a platform that allows the authors to bring compute to the data rather than the data to the compute. This fundamentally changes the economic model for working with Earth imagery, enabling the authors to analyze 3.3 million image tiles covering more than 100 terabytes of imagery across both countries. In their approach, all Landsat pixels across the world are processed using a deep learning algorithm called a Random forest, and a subset of the pixels are manually labeled according to the land cover class. Once trained, the Random forest algorithm is then applied to all pixels, producing a map of land cover classes for the entire globe.

## What a binary map can't tell you

The Random forest creates a binary map that indicates whether a pixel has cropland or not. It does not attempt to classify the type of cropland or the type of crop, whether the crop is irrigated or rain-fed, or any of the other kinds of distinctions that are useful to farmers and agricultural planners. But that’s fine, because the researchers aren’t trying to answer those questions. Instead, they’re trying to prove a point about scale and transferability.

## The payoff: one definition everywhere

What they’re trying to demonstrate is that a single methodology that allows accurate identification of croplands across very different countries opens up the possibility of comparing the different countries’ national agricultural statistics. And if the identification of croplands is accurate, and the methodology is transparent, then it’s also possible to identify historical trends in a comparable way. The researchers’ motivation for doing this kind of work comes from a different piece of research they did for China, in which they concluded that China’s cropland area had been overestimated by 20%. In a follow-up study, they found that the same bias existed in Australia.

# Breaking the Cycle in Kampala's Slums: A Case for Community-Owned Child Centers

In the slums of Kampala, a child can spend the whole day with no adult watching. Parents and guardians leave early to find work, and the children are left behind to fend for themselves. Nobody is responsible for where they go, what they eat, or what they run into.

The gap is sharpest for the most vulnerable: orphans, and the children of very young mothers. They have the fewest adults to turn to and the least margin for error. This article proposes a simple answer: child centers that are owned and run by the communities they serve.

## The cycle

The core of the problem is a cycle that repeats from one generation to the next. Poverty produces early motherhood, early motherhood limits a young woman's future, and her children inherit the same conditions.

Early motherhood is the entry point. A girl who becomes a mother young usually leaves school, and she often does so without reliable information about pregnancy, birth, or caring for a baby. Her options narrow before they have properly opened.

Her children then grow up unsupervised. Without a safe place to be, they face hazards that are part of daily life in the slums, and they have no adult close enough to step in.

The damage to nutrition and health does not fade with time. A child who goes hungry or sick in the early years carries that harm for life, and it limits what that child can learn, earn, and become. That puts the next generation in the same position as the last, and the cycle begins again.

This shapes the design of any serious response. If the cycle runs through young mothers and their unsupervised children, then a solution has to reach both at once. It cannot treat the children alone and leave the mothers where they are.

## Mothers are the lever

The distinctive move in this proposal is to treat caregivers as partners rather than as recipients. Mothers are not the problem to be managed. They are the people best placed to change what happens next.

That begins with safe-motherhood education aimed at young and first-time mothers. This goes straight to the cycle's entry point, where a lack of information and an interrupted education do the most damage. It also helps mothers while their children are still very young.

Alongside this, the centers offer skills and a way to earn income, so that mothers can support their families.

The payoff is that the cycle turns. A mother who is informed, skilled, and earning can keep her children healthier and give them more than she was given. What was a downward pattern becomes an upward one.

For the children, the centers provide play, learning, meals, and health care in one safe place.

This matters most for the most fragile children. Orphans and the children of very young mothers have the least support at home, so a dependable center can supply what is missing. For them, a place where adults are watching, feeding, and teaching can make the difference between falling into the cycle and breaking out of it.

## Why ownership decides whether it lasts

The centers should not belong to outside institutions. Programs run from afar tend to depend on those who run them, and they can disappear when attention or funding moves elsewhere. A center owned by its community has a different footing.

Local staff are the clearest mechanism. Hiring people from the community creates jobs for residents, which keeps income in the neighborhood. It also builds trust. Families are more willing to leave their children with people they know, and more willing to take advice from neighbors than from strangers.

Partners can then be folded in as an extension of this base. Outside organizations can add support, but they join something the community already holds rather than replacing it.

That is the real argument for ownership. The question is not only who runs the centers on opening day, but whether they are still running years later. A center that residents own, staff, and trust has a reason to continue. Sustainability is what lets a good idea become a lasting change, and it is why ownership has to stay with the community.

Dawn breaks over the sprawling slums of Bwaise and the dust coated toddlers stumble out of tin huts like ghosts in the early morning haze. They make their way through dirt alleyways to community-run child centers, which are quickly filling with the round-eyed bunches of wool. The youngest children are tended to by their mothers – many of whom are just pre-teens themselves – before setting off to their own makeshift schools. This chaotic scene may seem like normality, but it is only the sharpest edge of a much wider problem. The hazardous, unsupervised environment that children are leaving behind causes a lifetime of irreversible damage to their growth, health, education and livelihoods. In turn, this leads to greater poverty and further compromised health that perpetuates the cycle for another generation.

The proposal is to build community-owned and managed child centers that provide a safe space for learning, play, meals and health check-ups for children who are amongst the most vulnerable in Uganda. By focusing on the care of mothers and young children, the centers can provide a beacon of stability in a volatile environment that protects children from the most dangerous aspects of the slums. Further, it aims to address the root cause of the cycle by empowering mothers and their communities to develop their own sustainable solutions. This will not only ensure that the centers last, but will change the outlook of the children for whom they are intended.

The center will be built on three principles:

1. Safe motherhood education
2. Community ownership
3. Sustainable solutions

Firstly, the centers will provide safe motherhood education that is focused on pre- and newly-pregnant adolescents who are most at risk of dropping out of school and giving birth to unhealthy babies. In the first five years of life, 45% of deaths could be prevented by simple health and nutrition interventions. Therefore, the centers will provide essential education on hygiene, immunization and nutrition, as well as basic first aid and cooking skills to the mothers. They will also offer access to vital education on HIV/AIDS, contraception and family planning. The centers will provide an additional support network for both mothers and their children and will encourage positive community attitudes towards mothers and their children through regular social events.

In the second instance, this project aims to develop community ownership in Uganda by building a center that is run by and generates employment for young people from the community. The community will be involved in the center's design to ensure that it meets their needs. The center will provide a safe space for young people to learn the practical skills that will lead to sustainable employment, with the goal of developing transferable skills and giving them the best possible chance of securing formal employment. The center will also generate income from a range of activities including farming, breeding livestock and recycling waste. These will provide essential nutrition to the children in the center as well as generating income to employ local young people. Given the weak infrastructure in the slums, the center will also offer practical skills such as how to fix a leaky tap, or simple maintenance on cooking stoves. These skills will be taught to the mothers who bring their children to the center, while also improving the living conditions of the community.

Finally, the child centers will provide sustainable solutions for the problems facing Uganda's slums. The women and young people who run the centers will be fully trained in childcare and will provide both formal and informal education to children between the ages of 0-5 years. The centers will provide safe spaces for play and learning and will offer simple health checks and nutrition advice to the children. These centers will help to break the cycle of poverty by providing a safe space for children who would otherwise be left unsupervised, and will give them the best possible start in life. Further, the centers will provide employment for the next generation of young people in Uganda who are essential to the country's long-term development.

The impact of this project can be seen in the long-term. Beyond the immediate impact on the children who attend the centers, it will also help to break the cycle of poverty by empowering mothers and their communities to develop their own sustainable solutions. With this in mind, it is clear that this initiative will have a lasting and profound impact on the people of Uganda.

Kampala's slums have a large, and constantly expanding, population of mothers without partners. Very few of these mothers work. As a result, there is a supervision gap where neither parents nor teachers pay attention to the children. And that's the sharpest edge of the problem, the gap has allowed thousands of children to learn habits that do not get them on the right track to adulthood.

## The cycle

The problem is not that children don't attend school; there is something that happens before that, something that sets them off the track. The root of the problem is that, with children of very young mothers -who are more numerous than in any other place in the continent- there is a constant supervision gap. The gap is due to a combination of factors, early motherhood and unemployment, but the result is the same: children spend long hours unsupervised.
The problem is that, where a child should be spending time learning how to behave and grow into a responsible adult, they are left to fend for themselves, to learn from their peers only, with no guidance from parents, teachers or other adults. They are left to socialize among themselves, only with the company of other children. It is not that the children have nothing to do, it is that they have no guidance. This is the gap that their mothers fill in the afternoon, when they come back from work.
The gap allows children to learn habits that do not get them on the right track to adulthood. What happens in these neighborhoods is that children learn the wrong habits from each other, and they do that in an environment that is full of risks and hazards. The dangers are manifold, from getting run over to being exposed to drugs and violence, to less dangerous, but equally harmful, hazards such as malnutrition and health problems.
When a child suffers from malnutrition, it is not just that they are hungry for one day, and it is not that their education suffers only for one day. The impact of malnutrition goes on throughout their lives. Same for health problems; a child that is sick for one day in a poor neighborhood will not be able to go to school for several days, but, again, it is not only that, the impact goes on throughout their lives.

The solution is to address the root of the problem, the supervision gap. This can be addressed by involving the mothers as partners in the solution, by providing them with the skills and income that give them the means to be there for their children. When mothers are able to look after their children, both the mothers and the children benefit, but, more importantly, the community wins.
The project could target young, first-time mothers, providing them with safe-motherhood training and employment opportunities, but it should also provide the children with a safe and supervised space to play, learn, eat and get their health check. The project would have two goals, mothers and children. The project could also add a micro-finance training to its safe-motherhood program, to turn the employment opportunities into businesses that could be the means to further increase the mothers' income. In this way, the project would provide a one-stop solution, from safe-motherhood training and employment, to micro-finance training, and to child services, all in one place.

## Why ownership decides whether it lasts

The community will have to own the center if it is to last. There are no outside institutions that would pay the salaries indefinitely. The project could not survive without the mothers, it would not make sense if it wasn't owned by the mothers.
The project would have to be designed from the ground up to be owned by the mothers. From the day it opens, it should be designed so that the mothers can control it. It should provide jobs for local women, and it should be designed to give the mothers the means to own and run it.
The center would have to be designed with that in mind, not only to employ local women, but to give them the skills that would allow them to run and own it. The local staff would need to include a woman that would run the center from day one, and the center would have to be designed so that the mothers could run it on their own.
The project would not make sense unless it was designed to be owned by the mothers, it would not be sustainable unless it was designed so that the mothers could run it on their own.
The partners
The project would need partners, from start-up capital to support in implementing it. The partners would have to provide seed money, and the staff with training and advice. They would have to provide the equipment, from computers to sports equipment, and the materials, from toys to books, but they would also have to provide the local staff with training and advice.

# A Breed Made by Work

The dog drops low, eyes fixed on the sheep, and does not move. The sheep shift, bunch, and begin to walk where the dog wants them. There is no lunge, no bite, no chase. The dog never touches them. It simply holds their attention, and they go.

This is the thing worth understanding about the herding dog: it controls without force. The animal is working a hunting instinct, but the work looks nothing like hunting. Nearly everything that follows, including why the breed is so admired and why it can be so hard to live with, comes from that one fact.

## A hunt with the ending removed

Herding is a hunt with the ending removed. Selection did not invent new behavior so much as take the predatory sequence apart, cutting away the parts that end in a kill and sharpening the parts that move an animal from one place to another.

The most striking piece of what remains is the eye. It is pressure applied at a distance: the dog fixes its gaze on the stock and the stock responds to it, without any contact. The stalk is similarly transformed. Where a predator closes in to attack, the herding dog closes in to be felt. Its power is presence rather than force.

But the trait that makes the whole arrangement useful is the last one: responsiveness to the handler. A dog with eye and stalk but no interest in the person would simply be a predator that stops short. Attention to the handler is what turns predation into teamwork, aiming all that intensity at a shared task instead of at the dog's own appetite.

## Bred for ability, never for looks

The selection pressure on these dogs was performance, full stop. A dog was kept and bred because it could do the work. Eye, stalk, and responsiveness survived because they were what the work demanded.

Telfer is often credited with shaping the breed, though the history here is shaky. His point, as the story goes, was to fix traits in the dogs, not to fix a look.

That leads to the rule, which can be stated bluntly: if it works, it is the right dog, whatever it looks like. Appearance was never the standard, and the evidence is in plain sight. Look at the breed and you see varied coats and colors. Dogs that share almost nothing in appearance share the ability, because ability was all anyone was selecting for.

Working trials were the mechanism that enforced this, putting each dog's performance in front of people who could judge it.

## The same dog, indoors

Here the story turns, because the traits that make this dog superb at its job are the same ones that make it difficult at home. McConnell, a credentialed voice on the subject, makes the case for taking that seriously.

Put the dog in a house, and the predatory sequence does not switch off. It turns on the wrong targets. The eye, the stalk, and the urge to move things along attach themselves to children, cars, cats, and anything else that runs. The symptoms vary, but heel-nipping is the clearest example: a dog doing exactly what it was bred to do, to the wrong animal in the wrong place.

This is also a thinking dog, and a thinking dog without a job invents one. The work does not disappear just because no one has assigned it. The dog finds its own, and its choices are rarely ones a household would pick.

What it needs is real work, or something close enough to occupy both its body and its mind. A walk isn't enough. A walk exercises the legs and leaves the rest of the dog, the part that was bred for the work, with nothing to do.

A Breed Made by Work

## A hunt with the ending removed

I have no doubt that people need to breed a variety of dog with a higher instinct to kill than the average hunting dog, but I am also sure that if you test a lot of dogs, you will still find a lot that have a lot of killing instinct, perhaps not as much as a dog who was selected for the trait, but enough to kill. One of the things you have to do to bring out the killing instinct is to give the dog the opportunity to experience the thing that they are designed to kill. And so they will bring out the instinct to kill in a dog, and the instinct to kill in a dog is very strong if the dog is raised without this type of exposure. And I think the same thing is true with dogs that have been selected for some other trait. It is my experience that a dog will take to a job more easily if he is raised to do that job and has the instinct for that job than if he is selected for that job and has no instinct for that job. So if you want to breed a dog that is very responsive to his handler and takes to a job without a lot of pressure or force, you will have a much easier time of it if you select against dogs that are too responsive or take to a job too easily, and then work with the dog to bring out the trait you want. Because once you do that, the dog will take to the job with more gusto, and it will be easier to get him to respond to you. And that is the essence of what we are trying to do with the dog in our kennel.

## Bred for ability, never for looks

The dogs that we have today are all descendants of the original hunting dog that was brought to England from the continent. At that time, there was no official dog show, and the dogs were bred for their ability to do the job that they were bred for. And because of that, I think there is no doubt that the dogs that were selected for their ability to do their job were at least as good, if not better, than the dogs that were selected for their looks.
